newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: NKF sees recovery in medium-long term.
newsitem.headline: NKF sees recovery in medium-long term.

text.p: Dutch cable maker NKF Holding NV said on Wednesday it expected results to recover in the medium to long term after an expected profit fall in 1997.

"We expect a recovery and a growth of profits in the medium-long term to 2001," chairman Tonn van de Laar told a news conference on NKF's annual report. But he declined to say whether NKF expected to post a profit rise in 1998.

NKF said last February its 1996 net profit had risen by almost nine percent to 44.1 million guilders but shocked investors by adding that it expected a substantial profit fall in 1997, due to problems in the energy cables market in Germany.
Financial manager Robert de Bakker confirmed this implied an expected plunge of 1997 net profits of 30 to 45 percent.
Van de Laar said the German market for energy cables had been seriously hit by price erosion, and market prices now only covered 60 to 90 percent of manufacturers' production costs.
NKF had expected a price fall in this sector of about five percent in 1997, but in January alone the prices had already plunged 30 percent.
Only three big companies take up about half of the total demand in this market and are therefore able to dictate prices in a situation where suppliers have production overcapacity.
"The present price level is unrealistic, but it is a temporary phenomenon," Van de Laar said, adding that the first signals had already emerged that overcapacity was waning.
Some big market players in Germany, including NKF itself, had already cut back production levels or were planning to do so and smaller firms had moved to other product sectors.

NKF also cut its costs in Germany by laying off 50 temporary workers, about 15 percent of the German workforce. But Van de Laar said NKF could not cut costs at the same rate as market prices had fallen because its German unit NFK/Kaiser had already been reorganised in previous years.
Business in other market segments and geographical areas, notably in Finland, was much better and showed good prospects. Last year, NKF took over the cable division of Nokia.

Van de Laar said NKF had successfully moved further towards product sectors with higher added value. For the years ahead it expects fast growth in sectors such as the installation of local communication networks for big clients, video transmission equipment and glass fibres production.
Another sector where strong expansion is seen is the production of cables for mobile telecommunications stations, where NKF now has a global market share of 15 percent.
Last year, these highly profitable sectors generated about 10 percent of the 1.34 billion guilders group turnover but this is seen growing rapidly.
"We should be able to double this (the share of these sectors on total sales) in about three years," financial manager De Bakker said.
